raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide transient coronary support and antiproliferative drug delivery after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), followed by resorption and potential restoration of vasomotion, adaptive remodeling, improved imaging, and freedom from a permanent metallic cage. The concept is old: the Igaki-Tamai poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) scaffold showed feasibility in humans, but required heated balloon expansion and had limited antirestenotic capability [1]. The everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold established the modern BVS field. Early ABSORB cohort studies in selected, simple lesions showed acceptable late loss, healing, vasomotion, and no early signal for scaffold thrombosis, and long-term intravascular imaging demonstrated disappearance of struts and favorable vascular responses in small cohorts [2-6].

The randomized Absorb program initially supported clinical optimism. In ABSORB II, 1-year clinical outcomes were similar between BVS and cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (EES), but by 3 years the scaffold failed to show superior vasomotion and had more target-vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis [7,8]. ABSORB III met 1-year noninferiority for target-lesion failure in relatively noncomplex lesions [9], but 3-year and 5-year follow-up revealed an excess of target-lesion failure, target-vessel myocardial infarction, and scaffold thrombosis before complete resorption [10,11]. ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan also demonstrated angiographic noninferiority in selected lesions, but later follow-up and substudies reinforced concern about scaffold thrombosis and the importance of vessel sizing and lesion preparation [12,13]. The all-comers AIDA trial was particularly influential: it showed no reduction in target-vessel failure and a substantially higher rate of definite or probable device thrombosis with BVS [14]. ABSORB IV, which mandated more careful technique and excluded very small vessels, improved early outcomes but did not eliminate concerns [15].

Mechanistically, first-generation polymeric BVS had thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, lower radial strength than metallic EES, and slower resorption. These features predisposed to flow disturbance, malapposition, underexpansion, fracture, and late dismantling during polymer degradation. Consequently, “PSP” implantation—adequate lesion preparation, appropriate sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—became central to BVS practice [16]. Intravascular imaging studies from ABSORB Japan and related analyses showed that underexpansion, malapposition, calcification, and suboptimal embedment were modifiable contributors to adverse outcomes [17,18]. Meta-analyses consistently confirmed a higher risk of scaffold thrombosis, particularly beyond 1 year, compared with contemporary drug-eluting stents [19-21]. Expert consensus therefore emphasized avoidance of small vessels, heavy calcification, thrombotic lesions, long overlapping scaffolds, and discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy during the resorption phase [22].

The clinical failure of first-generation Absorb did not invalidate the bioresorbable concept; rather, it clarified design requirements. Next-generation scaffolds aim for thinner struts, faster and more predictable resorption, stronger acute radial support, larger expansion windows, better radiopacity, and simpler implantation. Magnesium-based scaffolds are attractive because metal permits improved mechanical behavior while resorbing faster than PLLA. The sirolimus-eluting DREAMS 2G/Magmaris platform showed favorable 6- and 12-month outcomes without definite or probable scaffold thrombosis in BIOSOLVE-II [23,24], and 5-year follow-up suggested sustained safety in selected lesions [25]. In the larger BIOSOLVE-IV registry, 2-year outcomes were reassuring, though events clustered in higher-risk scenarios and premature antiplatelet discontinuation remained relevant [26].

Other polymeric platforms have pursued thinner struts and alternative drugs. NeoVas, a sirolimus-eluting PLLA scaffold, was noninferior to metallic EES for 1-year angiographic late loss in a Chinese randomized trial [27]. The MeRes100 sirolimus-eluting scaffold and DESolve novolimus-eluting scaffold demonstrated feasibility in early studies and registries, with improved deliverability or resorption profiles, although definitive randomized outcome data remain limited [28-30].

In contemporary PCI, BVS should not be viewed as routine substitutes for modern ultrathin metallic drug-eluting stents, whose safety and efficacy are excellent. Their plausible niche remains younger patients, simple proximal lesions in adequately sized vessels, and situations where future surgical grafting, side-branch access, or restoration of vasomotion might be valuable. However, such theoretical advantages require proof in adequately powered trials using current-generation scaffolds, imaging-guided implantation, contemporary antiplatelet strategies, and long follow-up beyond resorption. The BVS story is therefore best interpreted as a cautionary but productive cycle of innovation: a compelling biological concept, premature clinical adoption, identification of failure mechanisms, and redesign toward safer transient coronary scaffolding.
